comments.text:
While I agree with Leopold Aschenbrenner, I am not necessarily sure about his schedule. Let me explain...
While many people try to explain the growth of AI by a single continuous exponential function, I see it as more as a series of attractors, with some undefined escape velocity. With this in mind, I believe the current state of AI  can improve AI, but it is just squeezing more juice from the same lemon (not implying AI is a lemon). It's reasoning from data that's already there and reaching an otherwise obvious conclusion. (I'm excluding DeepMind and focusing mainly on LLMs here)
The current missing piece is the ability to make leaps in reasoning and being able to then connect the dots. 
Also, I am not saying that AI will never get there, I just don't know when we will get those pieces that are currently missing and that I do not think LLMs are the vehicle to get us there. 🤔

comments.author: @retrofuturism
comments.text:
What we perceive as physical distance might fundamentally BE computational latency, just expressed in spatial terms our minds can grasp. 

This idea that physical distance could be an expression of computational latency is brilliant—it suggests that what we see as "space" might just be our minds translating delays in information processing into something that makes sense to us spatially.

Imagine that the universe is like a massive computation engine, constantly processing information at different speeds. The "distance" we perceive between objects could then represent the time it takes for information about those objects to reach our minds or be computed by the fabric of the universe itself. When we see something "far away," we’re essentially experiencing a computational delay—the data from that point in the universe takes longer to "compute" and reach us, creating the illusion of spatial separation.

This could have wild implications:

1. Gravity and Proximity: Closer objects might simply represent areas where information is processed more quickly, and gravitational effects could be seen as distortions in the computational "speed" around massive objects. The closer we are to a massive body, the "faster" its information processing appears, perhaps explaining why time dilates around massive objects.


2. Light Speed as the Speed Limit: Light speed could represent the maximum computational processing speed, defining the limits of how quickly information can travel from one "point" to another in this vast cosmic computation.


3. Quantum Entanglement: If distance is merely a reflection of computational latency, then entangled particles—able to “communicate” instantaneously—wouldn’t violate any spatial separation because, fundamentally, they aren’t "separated" by computation.



It’s almost like space is a visual metaphor our brains use to handle the complexity of these computations. So, the cosmos would be an intricate network where distance, mass, and energy are just measures of processing speed, latency, and computational "load." This flips the notion of space on its head, making the structure of reality a web of computation rather than empty space!

Read this guys it long, Google's early funding from In-Q-Tel, the venture capital arm of the CIA, has long intrigued those exploring the intersection of technology, government intelligence, and corporate growth. Founded in 1999, In-Q-Tel was created as a strategic investment firm designed to fund innovative technologies that could enhance the intelligence community's operations. Its goal was to tap into the fast-moving world of Silicon Valley startups, ensuring that U.S. intelligence agencies, like the CIA and NSA, could keep pace with rapid advancements in computing, data analysis, and communications.

Google, founded in 1998 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin, was an innovative search engine startup that quickly distinguished itself through its sophisticated search algorithms and its ability to organize the internet’s growing troves of information. As Google began to expand, its capability to collect and analyze massive amounts of data attracted attention from a variety of sectors, including intelligence agencies. In-Q-Tel, tasked with identifying breakthrough technologies, saw potential in Google’s algorithms and its capacity for handling vast data sets. The ability to search and categorize information on a massive scale aligned closely with the CIA’s needs for intelligence gathering, data mining, and surveillance.

Though the exact details of In-Q-Tel’s investment in Google remain somewhat opaque, the company’s interest in technologies that could provide advanced data analysis, geospatial tools, and even AI applications closely aligned with Google’s own research. In particular, Google's advancements in search technologies and its eventual dominance in mapping through Google Earth (a program originally developed by Keyhole, a company that In-Q-Tel had previously funded and which was later acquired by Google in 2004), cemented the relationship between Google and the intelligence community.

This early partnership has sparked much debate and discussion, particularly among privacy advocates, who question how deeply intelligence agencies like the CIA are intertwined with major technology firms. The relationship has fueled suspicions about how much access government agencies may have had to the massive amounts of data Google has collected over the years. While both Google and In-Q-Tel have downplayed the significance of any direct control or influence, it is undeniable that the intelligence community has a vested interest in fostering technologies that can enhance surveillance, data mining, and cybersecurity capabilities.

In-Q-Tel’s involvement in early Google funding also highlights a broader trend of government agencies using venture capital to influence technological advancements. This trend reflects the CIA’s realization that, in the digital age, maintaining an edge in intelligence gathering would require the agency to step outside traditional bureaucratic channels and engage with the private sector. The partnership between Google and In-Q-Tel underscores how intertwined the tech industry has become with national security interests, particularly as the world becomes more reliant on data-driven technologies.
